h1: Green Wedding Guest Dresses: From Emerald to Sage to Olive
intro: Green wedding guest dresses cover a wider range than almost any other color family, from pale sage at a spring garden ceremony to near-black forest green at a December black tie reception. Green has no etiquette problem attached to it; the only color rule that applies to every wedding guest is to avoid white. The real decision is which green, and that depends on the season, the hour and the formality on the invitation.

contentSections.heading: Which green? Sage, olive, emerald and dark green compared
contentSections.content:
"Green" covers four quite different dresses, and they suit different invitations. Sage is a soft gray-green that reads as a pastel; it belongs to daytime, spring and garden weddings. Olive is a muted yellow-brown green that sits with the autumn palette. Emerald is a deep, saturated blue-green that looks like a jewel tone and carries formal and evening dress codes well. Dark or forest green is close to black-green and is the most formal-looking of the four, a natural fit for black tie optional and winter evenings.

In our analysis of 10,700 posts from wedding guests asking whether an outfit works, 630 mentioned green. Sage was the most named shade (100 posts), followed by olive (69), dark or forest green (60) and emerald (54). This page now covers all four shades; the separate shade pages were merged into it so each green has one home.

contentSections.heading: Emerald: the green for formal invitations
contentSections.content:
Emerald is a deep, saturated blue-green with the presence of a jewel tone, and it is the shade that carries formality best. At black tie, an emerald floor-length gown in satin or heavy chiffon is a strong alternative to black and navy; A-line and column silhouettes work well because the color does most of the visual work, so keep the jewelry restrained. At cocktail and semi-formal weddings, an emerald midi or knee-length dress in crepe, velvet or structured satin holds the color well at shorter lengths.

Emerald works year-round and looks most at home from fall through winter. Gold jewelry is the classic pairing; black or metallic shoes keep it sharp. Velvet emerald under warm reception light is one of the richest looks available to a winter guest.

contentSections.heading: Sage and mint belong to daylight
contentSections.content:
Sage is a soft gray-green that behaves like a pastel. It sits naturally beside eucalyptus, white flowers, natural wood and linen, which makes it a fit for spring and summer garden, vineyard and outdoor daytime weddings. Mint is lighter and brighter again and stays firmly in spring and summer.

Choose fabrics that keep sage soft: chiffon, organza, lightweight crepe and silk. Heavy satin and velvet can make it look muddy, so save those for the deeper greens. Silver, rose gold or nude accessories suit sage's cool undertone better than yellow gold; blush shoes and bags are a gentle pairing, and burgundy or plum accessories give a stronger contrast if you wear sage into early fall.

Sage fades into the season after September. For October and November, move to olive, moss or forest green instead.

contentSections.heading: Olive is the autumn and rustic green
contentSections.content:
Olive is a muted yellow-brown green that belongs to the autumn palette and to relaxed venues: casual fall weddings, barns, vineyards and rustic outdoor celebrations. It is less formal than emerald or forest green and pairs naturally with warm materials, including brown or cognac leather, gold jewelry and tan shoes.

Olive works well in matte fabrics such as crepe, satin-back crepe, cotton blends and fine knits, and as a slip or midi with a leather or suede accessory at a daytime fall wedding. For a formal fall evening, move to a deeper shade, such as dark olive in velvet or forest green in satin.

contentSections.heading: Dark and forest green: the formal alternative to black
contentSections.content:
Forest, hunter and pine greens sit close to black-green and are the most formal-looking greens. They fit black tie optional and black tie evenings and are seasonal from September through February. In velvet, heavy satin or brocade, a dark green midi or gown looks rich without reading as a holiday costume, especially at a winter wedding that is not Christmas-themed.

Pair dark green with gold, brown or warm neutral accessories, or black for a sharper effect. At a December wedding, avoid pairing it with bright red accessories unless the couple has asked for a red-and-green palette.

Whatever the shade, check the wedding party's colors: the only real way for green to go wrong is to match the bridesmaids.

faqs.question: Can I wear green to a wedding?
faqs.answer: Yes. Green has no etiquette rule against it; the color guests are asked to avoid is white, and green is nowhere near it. Choose the shade for the season and dress code, and check the bridesmaids' color so you do not match them.

faqs.question: Can I wear sage green to a fall wedding?
faqs.answer: In September, yes. For late October and November, sage starts to look like a spring color, so move to olive, moss, emerald or forest green, which suit the season and the heavier fabrics it calls for.

faqs.question: Is green appropriate for a black tie wedding?
faqs.answer: Yes, in a deep shade and a formal fabric. An emerald or forest green floor-length gown in satin or velvet suits black tie, and The Emily Post Institute's black tie list also includes a dressy cocktail dress, so a very dressy emerald cocktail dress works too.

faqs.question: What color shoes go with a green wedding guest dress?
faqs.answer: Nude and tan are the most versatile, gold suits emerald, olive and forest green, and silver or blush suits sage and mint. Black gives deep greens a sharp finish. Avoid shoes in a slightly different green unless it is a deliberate tonal match.
